Assertions::Assertions.summary: Use toBe for primitive values and shared object references, toEqual for recursive structural comparison, and specialized matchers for conditions such as array contents or thrown errors. Add .not to negate any matcher.
Assertions::Assertions.explanation: Vitest assertions start with expect and finish with a matcher. Use toBe for primitive equality or the same object reference, toEqual for recursively comparing structure, and specialized matchers such as toContainEqual or toThrow when the condition is more specific.

parameters.name: received
parameters.description: Value received by expect and compared by the matcher.

parameters.name: value / expected
parameters.description: Expected value or comparison argument; toBe accepts a value and toEqual accepts the expected value.

example.title: Choosing assertion matchers
example.code:
import { expect, test } from 'vitest'

test('uses the right matcher', () => {
  expect(2 + 2).toBe(4)
  expect({ id: 1, name: 'Ada' }).toEqual({ id: 1, name: 'Ada' })
  expect([1, { id: 2 }]).toContainEqual({ id: 2 })
  expect(() => { throw new Error('bad input') }).toThrow('bad input')
})
example.explanation: The test uses primitive equality, recursive structural equality, array-item structural matching, and an error matcher.

useCases.title: Primitive equality
useCases.scenario: Checking numbers, strings, or booleans against exact expected values.

useCases.title: Structural equality
useCases.scenario: Comparing returned objects or arrays by their nested contents.

useCases.title: Array item matching
useCases.scenario: Verifying that an array contains an object with selected structure.

useCases.title: Error assertions
useCases.scenario: Checking that a function throws the expected error.

keyPoints: Start with an exact-equality matcher when the expected value should match precisely.
toBe uses Object.is semantics, making it suitable for primitive values and exact references.
Prefer toBe for numbers, strings, booleans, and other primitive comparisons.
toEqual compares nested object and array contents recursively without requiring the same object reference.
Choose toStrictEqual when explicit undefined properties, sparse arrays, or object types must also match.
Prefix a matcher with .not to assert that the condition is false.
gotchas: Do not use toBe to compare separately created objects that merely have identical properties; it checks object identity.
For an object inside an array, use toContainEqual rather than toContain.

Async testing::Testing promises.summary: Test promise outcomes by awaiting `.resolves` or `.rejects` assertions. Async test callbacks are awaited by Vitest, while assertion-count guards help detect asynchronous paths that never run.
Async testing::Testing promises.explanation: Make the test callback async and await promise-based assertions. Use `.resolves` to unwrap a successful result and `.rejects` to check its rejection reason; awaiting them ensures Vitest observes the assertion before the test finishes.

parameters.name: received
parameters.description: A promise, or an async function supplied for rejection testing, followed by `.resolves` or `.rejects` and a matcher.

parameters.name: matcher arguments
parameters.description: The expected resolved value, rejection reason, or error characteristics accepted by the selected matcher.

Async testing::Testing promises.returns: The asynchronous matcher returns a Promise that must be awaited.

example.title: Testing resolved and rejected promises
example.explanation: The test awaits both asynchronous assertions: one checks the resolved value and the other verifies the expected rejection.

useCases.title: Successful promise results
useCases.scenario: Verify that an async operation returns the expected object or value.

useCases.title: Expected rejection paths
useCases.scenario: Confirm that invalid input or missing data produces the intended error.

useCases.title: Assertion execution checks
useCases.scenario: Protect callback- or chain-based tests from passing without executing assertions.

keyPoints: An async test function is awaited by Vitest, so returning or awaiting its promise keeps the test open until asynchronous work completes.
Use `.resolves` for successful outcomes and `.rejects` for expected failures instead of manually unpacking the promise.
After unwrapping, ordinary matchers such as `toMatchObject` or `toThrow` validate the resulting value or error.
Use `expect.assertions(n)` when a test must execute a known number of assertions, especially across asynchronous callbacks.
gotchas: Always await `.resolves` and `.rejects` assertions; otherwise the test can finish before the assertion is properly observed.
Assertions hidden in callbacks or promise chains may never run, so asynchronous tests can pass without checking anything.
Expected rejections must be handled with `.rejects` or an explicit catch; unhandled rejected promises fail the test run.

Configuration::Environment and globals.summary: Configure the runtime available to tests and decide whether Vitest APIs are global. Node is the default; use jsdom for browser-like APIs and enable globals only when desired.
Configuration::Environment and globals.explanation: Vitest runs tests in Node by default. Set `test.environment` to `jsdom` when browser APIs are needed, and set `test.globals` to `true` only when tests should use Vitest APIs globally instead of importing them.

parameters.name: test.environment
parameters.description: Selects the runtime used for test files; supported values include `node`, `jsdom`, `happy-dom`, `edge-runtime`, or a string custom environment name.

parameters.name: test.globals
parameters.description: Controls whether Vitest APIs are exposed globally; defaults to `false`.

example.title: Configure a browser-like environment and globals
example.explanation: This configuration supplies browser-like APIs and makes Vitest APIs available without imports.

useCases.scenario: Unit tests for server-side code that should use the standard Node runtime.

useCases.title: Browser-like tests
useCases.scenario: Component or DOM tests that need browser-like APIs such as `window` and `document`.

useCases.title: Global test APIs
useCases.scenario: Teams that prefer Jest-style global `test`, `expect`, and related Vitest APIs.

keyPoints: Use `test.environment` to select the runtime environment for tests.
The environment accepts built-in names such as `node` and `jsdom`, as well as custom environment names.
Web application tests can use `jsdom` or `happy-dom` for browser-like APIs.
The environment can also be selected from the command line.
Enable global Vitest APIs with the CLI option or the `globals: true` configuration setting.
gotchas: Global APIs are disabled by default, so enabling `globals` changes the explicit-import behavior.
Choose `jsdom` explicitly for browser-oriented tests; otherwise tests use Node.
TypeScript projects using global Vitest APIs must add the corresponding type declarations.

Configuration::Test projects.summary: Test projects let one Vitest process run unit, browser, integration, or other suites with different configurations. Define projects inline or reference project config files and globs, while inline projects can inherit shared root setup.
Configuration::Test projects.explanation: Vitest lets one process run multiple test projects, each with its own configuration. Define them in the root test.projects array as inline configurations, config files, or glob-based references; inline projects can inherit the root configuration so shared setup is reused while project-specific options distinguish unit, browser, and integration tests.

parameters.name: test.projects
parameters.description: An array containing inline project configurations, config-file paths, or glob patterns.

example.title: Separate test projects with shared configuration
example.explanation: This root configuration defines separate unit, browser, and integration projects while inline projects inherit the shared root setup.

useCases.title: Monorepo testing
useCases.scenario: A monorepo has packages with separate Vitest configurations.

useCases.title: Separate test types
useCases.scenario: Unit, browser, and integration tests need different environments or file patterns.

useCases.title: Configuration-specific suites
useCases.scenario: Several suites need distinct aliases, plugins, or browser settings.

keyPoints: Use test.projects to run several differently configured test groups in one Vitest process.
Projects suit monorepos and suites needing distinct aliases, plugins, environments, or browser settings.
A project can be declared inline, through a configuration file, or with a glob pattern.
Inline projects keep related configuration in the root file and are useful for small, focused test groups.
Inline projects and referenced project configurations may be combined in one projects array.

Quality::Coverage providers.summary: Select V8, Istanbul, or a custom provider for coverage collection, then enforce global or glob-specific thresholds. Positive values require minimum percentages; negative values cap uncovered items.
Quality::Coverage providers.explanation: Vitest collects coverage through a selected provider and can enforce global or file-pattern thresholds. Positive threshold values require at least that percentage; negative values instead limit how many items may remain uncovered.

parameters.description: Coverage provider: v8, istanbul, or custom.

useCases.title: Instrumented coverage
useCases.scenario: Use Istanbul when instrumented coverage is preferred or required by the project.

useCases.title: CI quality gates
useCases.scenario: Set global minimums to make CI fail when coverage drops below the target.

useCases.title: Glob-specific thresholds
useCases.scenario: Apply stricter or different requirements to selected source-file groups.

keyPoints: Choose V8, Istanbul, or a custom provider according to the runtime and reporting needs.
If no provider is configured, Vitest uses V8.
Set test.coverage.provider in vitest.config.ts to select the built-in provider.
Positive thresholds define the minimum required percentage for the selected coverage metric.
Negative thresholds express an allowed count of uncovered items rather than a percentage.
Glob-pattern thresholds let different file groups have separate requirements.
gotchas: V8 and Istanbul coverage support are optional dependencies, so install the provider package required by the chosen configuration.
Uncovered source files do not appear automatically; configure coverage.include when the report must include them.
The V8 provider requires a JavaScript runtime built on V8, such as Node.js, Deno, or Chromium-based browsers.

Test doubles::Mock factories.summary: Mock factories let `vi.mock` replace a module with controlled exports returned by a reusable factory. The factory runs once, is cached, and is applied before imports so tests stay deterministic.
Test doubles::Mock factories.explanation: A mock factory is the second argument to `vi.mock`; it returns the replacement module exports. Vitest evaluates that factory once, caches its result for later imports, and runs the hoisted mock before imports, so tests receive the same controlled dependency implementation.

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: Module path or dynamic import identifying the module to replace.

parameters.name: factory
parameters.description: Optional factory that returns replacement exports, or mock options such as `spy`.

example.title: Mock a module with a factory
example.explanation: The factory replaces the database module with a reusable fake whose controlled result makes the test deterministic.

useCases.title: Isolate external dependencies
useCases.scenario: Replace a database, API client, or filesystem adapter with predictable exports.

useCases.title: Make outcomes deterministic
useCases.scenario: Return a fixed value or controlled spy for a dependency used by the unit under test.

useCases.title: Build partial mocks
useCases.scenario: Reuse a module-shaped fake across tests while retaining selected real behavior.

useCases.title: Observe real exports
useCases.scenario: Track calls without replacing real implementations by choosing the documented spy option.

keyPoints: Pass a factory as the second argument to `vi.mock` to define the replacement module dynamically.
Every import of the mocked module receives the exports returned by the factory.
The factory can access the real module when a partial mock needs to preserve selected behavior.
Factories may perform asynchronous setup before returning replacement exports.
A spy option is an alternative when tracking real exports is preferable to defining a replacement factory.
gotchas: Place the call at top level and do not rely on its visual position: Vitest hoists it and executes it before imports.
Factory state is shared by later imports until the module is explicitly unmocked or dynamically unmocked.
A factory mock does not replace dependencies loaded through CommonJS `require`.
An asynchronous factory is supported, so the replacement module may be produced with awaited setup.

Test doubles::Mocked modules.summary: Mock imported modules with `vi.mock`, optionally supplying a factory for replacement exports. Vitest hoists the call before imports, so the mock is registered at the module boundary.
Test doubles::Mocked modules.explanation: `vi.mock` replaces a module's imported exports with either automatically generated mocks or the object returned by a factory. Vitest hoists the call before static imports, so the substitute is registered before dependent code loads. Use a factory for explicit behavior, and use `{ spy: true }` when exports should retain their implementations while being tracked.

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: Module path to replace; it may be a path or dynamic import expression.

parameters.name: factory
parameters.description: Optional factory returning the replacement module exports.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional options object; `{ spy: true }` preserves implementations while tracking exports.

example.title: Mock a module at its import boundary
example.explanation: The module import is replaced with a factory-created export before the test runs.

useCases.title: Isolate dependencies
useCases.scenario: Replace a database client or HTTP adapter so tests run without external I/O.

useCases.title: Control test inputs
useCases.scenario: Provide deterministic exports for a module whose real behavior is slow or environment-dependent.

useCases.title: Spy without replacement
useCases.scenario: Track calls while retaining real implementations.

useCases.title: Share a module mock
useCases.scenario: Apply the same module mock across tests from a setup file.

keyPoints: Use `vi.mock` to replace every imported export from a target module at the module boundary.
A factory gives the mocked module an explicit export object and behavior.
Without a factory, Vitest can use a matching adjacent `__mocks__` implementation.
Mock registration occurs before imports, enabling dependent modules to receive the substitute.
The module path may use aliases configured for the Vite project.
The API applies to ESM-style imports, not CommonJS loading.
gotchas: The call is moved ahead of imports, so writing it inside a test or setup block does not make it run there; keep it at top level.
CommonJS `require` imports are not supported by this API.
Putting the call in an imported module may prevent the expected hoisting behavior.
Factory output is shared and cached until the module is explicitly unmocked.

Test doubles::vi.fn and spies.summary: vi.fn creates a standalone mock function for callbacks or replacements, while vi.spyOn wraps an existing object method or accessor. Both track calls and share mock APIs; spies preserve the original implementation until overridden.
Test doubles::vi.fn and spies.explanation: Use vi.fn to create a standalone mock function, optionally with an implementation, and inspect its calls through mock properties or expect assertions. Use vi.spyOn to wrap an existing object method or accessor: it tracks calls while retaining the original behavior until you override it, and a spy can later restore the original member.
Test doubles::vi.fn and spies.syntax:
vi.fn(fn?: Function)
vi.spyOn<T, K extends keyof T>(object: T, method: K, accessType?: 'get' | 'set')

parameters.name: fn
parameters.description: Optional function implementation used by the standalone mock.

parameters.name: object
parameters.description: Object containing the method or accessor to wrap.

parameters.name: method
parameters.description: Property key identifying the method or accessor.

parameters.name: accessType
parameters.description: Optional accessor mode for a getter or setter.

Test doubles::vi.fn and spies.returns: vi.fn returns a Mock; vi.spyOn returns a MockInstance.

example.title: Tracking and replacing calls
example.explanation: The first test observes an existing method, temporarily changes its result, and restores it; the second creates a standalone mock callback.

useCases.title: Examine invocation history
useCases.scenario: Inspect returned values, thrown results, arguments, or instances recorded by a mock.

keyPoints: vi.fn creates a standalone mock function whose execution can be tracked.
Use vi.spyOn when the target is an existing object method or property.
The two APIs expose the same mock-control and inspection methods.

Test doubles::vi.mock.summary: `vi.mock` replaces a module's imports with a factory-defined module or an automatically mocked version. The call is hoisted before imports; `{ spy: true }` preserves export implementations while tracking calls.
Test doubles::vi.mock.explanation: `vi.mock` replaces a module at the import boundary. Vitest hoists the call before imports; an optional factory defines the replacement exports, while `{ spy: true }` keeps implementations intact and tracks calls. Prefer the dynamic-import form when supplying a factory.
Test doubles::vi.mock.syntax: vi.mock(path: string, factory?: () => unknown, options?: { spy?: boolean }): void

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: Module path or dynamic import identifying the module to mock; configured Vite aliases are supported.

parameters.name: factory
parameters.description: Optional factory returning replacement exports, or an options object such as `{ spy: true }`.

Test doubles::vi.mock.returns: The documentation does not specify a return value.

example.title: Mock a module export
example.explanation: The factory replaces the imported module and supplies a trackable mock implementation for its export.

useCases.title: Isolate external dependencies
useCases.scenario: Replace a database client, logger, or other dependency with controlled exports during a test.

useCases.title: Control module behavior
useCases.scenario: Return deterministic values from imported functions without invoking the real implementation.

useCases.title: Spy on a complete module
useCases.scenario: Track calls to every export while retaining the module's original implementations.

useCases.title: Configure setup-wide mocks
useCases.scenario: Apply the same module replacement automatically across test files.

keyPoints: Use it to replace every import from a target module with a mock module.
The module path may use aliases configured in Vite.
A factory controls the complete set of exports returned to importing code.
The second argument can configure spying without defining replacement exports.
`{ spy: true }` tracks exports while preserving their original behavior.
Hoisting makes the mock active before imported code is evaluated.
gotchas: The call runs before imports regardless of where it appears in the test file.
It does not mock modules loaded with `require()`.
Mocks in setup files may arrive too late for modules already cached.
A factory result is cached until the module is explicitly unmocked.

Test doubles::vi.stubGlobal.summary: Replace a global variable with a controlled test value. Restore it manually with vi.unstubAllGlobals() or configure Vitest to restore globals automatically before each test.

Restore stubs manually with vi.unstubAllGlobals(), or enable unstubGlobals in configuration for automatic restoration before each test.

Directly assigning to globalThis or window bypasses Vitest's restoration tracking; use vi.stubGlobal when restoration is needed.

Test foundations::Test and describe.explanation: Use `test` to declare a named case and keep its assertions in the callback. Wrap related cases in `describe` to form a suite; suites can also provide shared lifecycle setup and teardown through hooks.

afterAll registers cleanup that runs once after the current file or suite finishes.

afterEach registers work that runs after every test in the current suite.

Use named `setup` and `teardown` exports for explicit startup and cleanup phases.

Test hooks::Hook execution order.summary: In nested describe blocks, outer beforeEach hooks run before inner beforeEach hooks. After the test, inner afterEach hooks run before outer afterEach hooks, creating an outer-to-inner setup and inner-to-outer cleanup sequence.

For each nested test, outer beforeEach hooks run before inner beforeEach hooks; after the test, inner afterEach hooks run before outer afterEach hooks. beforeAll and afterAll run once for the suite rather than for every test.

beforeAll(fn, timeout?)

useCases.title: Suite-level lifecycle
useCases.scenario: Use suite-wide initialization and teardown when work should happen only once.

useCases.title: Debug hook order

keyPoints: Hooks at an outer level surround hooks declared in nested suites.
For setup, the outer beforeEach executes before the nested suite's beforeEach.
Inner setup runs after outer setup, allowing it to build on the broader context.
Cleanup starts with the innermost afterEach hook.
The outer afterEach runs last, after nested cleanup is complete.
Suite-wide hooks run once rather than once per test.
gotchas: By default, after hooks run in reverse stack order, so cleanup proceeds from the innermost scope outward.
A hook inside describe does not affect tests outside that suite.
Top-level hooks wrap tests throughout the file, including tests in nested suites.

Test hooks::Hook timeouts.summary: Give an individual hook its own timeout in milliseconds instead of increasing the default for every hook. This is useful when one setup or cleanup operation is slower than the rest.
Test hooks::Hook timeouts.explanation: Pass a timeout in milliseconds as the optional second argument to a hook such as beforeEach or afterEach. Vitest uses that value only for the selected hook, while the global hookTimeout remains the default for hooks without an override.
Test hooks::Hook timeouts.syntax:
beforeEach(fn, timeout?)
afterEach(fn, timeout?)
beforeAll(fn, timeout?)
afterAll(fn, timeout?)

parameters.name: fn
parameters.description: Callback executed by the hook.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Maximum wait before Vitest terminates the hook, in milliseconds.

Test hooks::Hook timeouts.returns: No return value is documented for the timeout option.

keyPoints: Hook APIs accept an optional timeout in milliseconds.
Use the timeout with `beforeEach` when setup needs more time.
Use the timeout with `afterEach` when cleanup needs more time.
Hooks default to 10 seconds unless a local timeout or global configuration changes it.
gotchas: A per-hook timeout overrides the default for that hook; `hookTimeout` changes the default globally.
For hooks that wrap a test, setup and teardown are timed independently.

Test hooks::Setup files.summary: Use test.setupFiles to run shared initialization before every test file. Paths are resolved from the project root, and multiple setup files can be ordered through sequence.setupFiles.
Test hooks::Setup files.explanation: Set test.setupFiles to one path or an array of paths. Vitest resolves those paths from the project root and executes the files before each test file, in the test process and before collection begins. Use setup files for reusable initialization such as polyfills, global configuration, and custom matchers; they are not meant to provide imports or exports to test files.

parameters.name: test.setupFiles
parameters.description: A path or paths to setup modules, resolved relative to the project root.

keyPoints: Each configured path is resolved relative to the project root.
A setup file runs before every test file and shares its process with the tests.
Multiple setup files are ordered by default; use sequence.setupFiles to control their scheduling.
Register shared pre-test code through the test.setupFiles configuration option.
Setup files execute before test collection, making them suitable for initialization that must precede collection.
gotchas: Exports from a setup file are not made available to test files; put shared values in another module and import that module where needed.
Disabling isolation does not make setup run only once: the setup file still executes before every test file, although imported modules are cached.
In watch mode, changing a setup file reruns the entire test suite.
